results.title: Real-World Classification of Pain States in Multiple Sclerosis Patients using Wearable Sensor Data and Ensemble Machine Learning
results.summary: <jats:p>Introduction: Pain assessment remains challenging due to its subjective nature and reliance on self-reports. These challenges are particularly relevant for multiple sclerosis (MS) patients, for whom pain is among the most common and fluctuating symptoms, occurring in multiple forms. Wearable sensors combined with machine learning (ML) offer the potential for continuous and more objective pain monitoring by leveraging physiological signals in real-world contexts. Methods: We monitored 18 MS patients over 48 h using the Empatica E4 wristband to collect photoplethysmography, electrodermal activity, skin temperature, and accelerometer data. Physiological features were extracted from 5-, 10-, and 15-min time windows preceding hourly self-reported pain assessment during waking hours. Univariate associations with pain states were evaluated using linear mixed effects models, correcting for multiple comparisons. For classification purposes, feature selection was performed via recursive feature elimination, and 5 ML algorithms were trained and tested with leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. Model performance was evaluated using the F1 score and the sensitivity-specificity balance. Results: For univariate analysis, after correction, only 2 out of 43 features showed significant differences between pain and no-pain states. For the classification task, models based on 5-min windows generally performed the best. The highest F1 score (0.78) was achieved by a Support Vector Machine using 2 features from 5-min windows, while XGBoost achieved the best sensitivity-specificity balance (0.69/0.68) with 2 features from 15-min windows. Conclusion: Wearable physiological signals may contain information relevant to pain-state classification in people with MS. However, these results should be considered preliminary, requiring validation in larger, independent cohorts to establish the robustness and generalizability of the proposed approach.</jats:p>

results.title: Altered network organization with shift to local processing during adaptive behaviour in multiple sclerosis
results.summary:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
<jats:p>To adjust to changing environmental demands, the brain needs to organize and (re)configure mental resources in so-called task sets. Following a network perspective of cognitive functions, these processes are considered to rely on dynamic exchange of information between distant brain regions, possibly synchronized by slow-wave theta oscillations. However, few attempts have been made to describe the directional transfer of information in theta networks during behavioural adaptation. In the current study, we examined directed neural information transfer in 57 healthy individuals and 57 patients with multiple sclerosis with a focus on brain–behaviour associations during task switching. For this, we calculated behavioural switch costs and further applied an artificial neural network-based approach on neurophysiological EEG data to estimate linear and non-linear effective connectivity measures within cortical networks during task switching. Source reconstruction and connectivity analyses revealed distinct neural network architectures and communication strategies during task switching in healthy controls compared to patients with multiple sclerosis. In healthy controls, enhanced modulations of long-range fronto-parietal connectivities were associated with higher reaction time switch costs, possibly reflecting increased cognitive demands rather than adaptive processes. In contrast, patients with multiple sclerosis relied more strongly on local intra-regional modulations, which is consistent with the idea of a dysconnectivity syndrome in multiple sclerosis. Strikingly, stronger modulations in self-connectivities were associated with better accuracy measures in patients with multiple sclerosis, suggesting a compensatory mechanism to support performance. Notably, only non-linear directed connectivity measures were related to behavioural switch costs, emphasizing the importance of non-linear models for adaptive cognitive processes.</jats:p>

results.title: Digital Twins in Clinical Neurology: From Concept to Clinical Application in Multiple Sclerosis
results.summary:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
<jats:p>Patient digital twins (DT) are emerging as a promising paradigm for personalised and predictive healthcare. In neurology, and particularly in multiple sclerosis (MS), the availability of longitudinal, multimodal data provides a strong foundation for developing patient‐specific digital models, including simulation‐based and mechanistic approaches. However, it remains unclear to what extent current approaches represent integrated, clinically embedded DT systems.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
<jats:p>We conducted a narrative review to synthesise current concepts, modelling approaches and translational challenges of DT in neurology, using MS as an illustrative use case. Existing approaches were mapped to core DT components, including data integration, predictive modelling, dynamic updating and clinical integration.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Results</jats:title>
<jats:p>Current DT‐related approaches in MS demonstrate substantial progress across complementary development tracks, including multimodal data integration, predictive modelling, digital biomarkers, mechanistic simulations, virtual‐patient frameworks and in silico trials. These capabilities represent important building blocks of DT development but have not yet been fully integrated into continuously operating clinical systems. Core DT functionalities, including continuous bidirectional data exchange, real‐time model updating and closed‐loop interaction with clinical workflows, remain limited. Key challenges include data fragmentation, limited interoperability, lack of standardised validation, and regulatory, ethical and economic constraints.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
<jats:p>MS represents a highly suitable model domain for DT development. Future progress will depend on further maturing and validating individual modelling and data‐integration capabilities, as well as on their integration into continuously updating, clinically embedded systems. Robust validation, scalable infrastructures and appropriate governance frameworks will be essential to establish safe, effective and clinically actionable use in practice.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>

results.title: Fifteen-year real-world pharmacovigilance of multiple sclerosis disease-modifying therapies: adverse event profiles, drug-specific safety signals and clinical implications
results.summary:
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Background</jats:title>
<jats:p>Disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) are the cornerstone of remission-phase management for multiple sclerosis (MS), a prevalent autoimmune neuroinflammatory disorder of the central nervous system. However, their immune-modulating mechanisms carry inherent risks of systemic and neurological adverse events (ADEs), which remain a major barrier to optimal long-term care. This study aimed to comprehensively characterize the real-world safety profiles of all major MS DMT classes and identify clinically actionable safety signals.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
<jats:p>We analyzed 15-year (2009Q1–2023Q4) ADE reports for 8 classes of FDA-approved MS DMTs from the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database. Four disproportionality algorithms (ROR, PRR, BCPNN, MGPS) were used for signal detection. Time-to-onset (TTO) analysis with Weibull distribution and multivariate logistic regression were performed to assess temporal risk patterns and patient-specific risk factors for important medical events (IMEs).</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Results</jats:title>
<jats:p>A total of 498,847 ADE reports (1,048,575 events) were included, with nearly 50% involving IMEs. The most common ADEs were systemic symptoms, infections, liver injury and alopecia. Notably, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML, ROR = 15.59) and spontaneous abortion (ROR = 2.54) were identified as high-risk severe events. Drug-specific analysis revealed distinct safety signatures: anti-CD20 antibodies carried the highest infection risk, natalizumab was strongly associated with PML (ROR = 45.62), and teriflunomide had the highest alopecia risk (ROR = 12.73). Approximately 70% of IMEs occurred within 2 years of treatment initiation. Multivariate analysis identified older age, male sex and longer treatment duration as independent risk factors for IMEs, while obesity was a protective factor.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
<jats:p>This long-term FAERS-based analysis identified potential safety signals associated with major MS DMTs, providing hypothesis-generating evidence to support clinical vigilance and prioritize further validation, but not to estimate incidence, comparative risk, or causality.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>

Aubagio is a medicine that contains the active substance teriflunomide. It is used to treat patients from the age of 10 years with multiple sclerosis (MS), a disease in which inflammation destroys the protective sheath around the nerves. 

Aubagio is used in the type of MS known as relapsing-remitting MS, when the patient has flare-ups of symptoms (relapses) followed by periods of recovery (remissions).

results.title: Identification of BRD4 as a Shared Diagnostic Biomarker Between Bipolar Disorder and Multiple Sclerosis Using Machine Learning.
results.summary: Bipolar disorder (BD) is closely associated with multiple sclerosis (MS), but their shared molecular mechanisms and specific diagnostic biomarkers remain unclear. This study integrated microarray expression profiling and machine learning to identify shared core genes and underlying mechanisms between BD and MS. Gene expression datasets and peripheral-blood transcriptome datasets were obtained from the GEO database. After per-cohort quantile normalization, shared genes were identified by differential expression analysis and weighted gene co-expression network analysis. A protein-protein interaction network was constructed, and key genes were screened using the MCODE plugin. Three machine learning algorithms were combined to identify the final core gene. A total of 229 shared genes were initially obtained and further filtered to 55 key genes. BRD4 was identified as the final shared core gene. Discriminative performance (AUC, 95% CI) was: BD discovery GSE23848 (20 cases/15 controls) 0.713 (0.54-0.89); MS discovery GSE21942 (12/15) 0.998 (0.99-1.00); BD external GSE39653 (8/24) 0.775 (0.59-0.96); MS external GSE203241 (38/21) 0.828 (0.71-0.93). BRD4 shows moderate-to-good discriminative performance as a non-invasive peripheral biomarker and may aid further investigation of shared BD-MS mechanisms.

results.title: Salivary Proteomics Reveals Disease- and Therapy-Associated Molecular Patterns in Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis.
results.summary: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic immune-mediated disease for which non-invasive biomarkers, able to detect disease- and treatment-associated molecular changes, are needed. We characterized the whole-saliva proteome of patients with relapsing-remitting (RR) MS at baseline before treatment initiation (MS-T0; n = 66) and after six months of disease-modifying therapy (MS-T1; n = 40), in comparison with healthy controls (HC; n = 31). Nano-liquid chromatography-high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry identified 1305 proteins, of which 209 differed among the main comparisons. Pairwise and paired analyses distinguished persistent RRMS-associated alterations, baseline-attenuation patterns with changes shifting towards HC levels, treatment-associated differences emerging at MS-T1, and longitudinal-only alterations. The identified patterns are descriptive and cannot be interpreted as evidence of pharmacological treatment effects or clinical response. The existence of specific RRMS alterations was supported by exploratory Random Forest, which classified HC, MS-T0 and MS-T1 samples using a panel of 50 proteins, most of which (96%) also showed significant changes in univariate tests. Reactome enrichment evidenced that proteins pertaining to the identified patterns are mainly involved in innate immunity, neutrophil degranulation, cell-death pathways, cytokine signalling, and protein folding. These findings indicate that six months of therapy was associated with substantial salivary proteome changes and support saliva as a candidate biofluid for longitudinal molecular monitoring and non-invasive detection of treatment-associated salivary proteome variations in RRMS.

results.title: A Comparative Review and Benchmarking Evaluation of Step Detection Methods for Longitudinal Gait Assessment
results.summary: <jats:p>Gait analysis based on inertial measurement units (IMUs) enables scalable longitudinal gait assessment, with step detection as a foundational component. However, an understanding of available step detection methods and their comparative performance across sensor placements, clinical populations, and real-world environments remains limited. This paper addresses this gap through a twofold contribution. First, a structured taxonomic review organises the landscape into six families—rule-based heuristics, phase portrait, template matching, time–frequency analysis, adaptive oscillators, and machine learning—characterising the trade-offs of each in terms of noise robustness, generalisability, and computational efficiency. Second, nine algorithms drawn from five of these families, all but phase portrait, are benchmarked across three large datasets encompassing healthy adults and people with mobility-impairing conditions such as Parkinson’s disease and multiple sclerosis, at multiple sensor placements under both controlled laboratory and free-living conditions. Accuracy depended on sensor placement, gait pathology and recording environment: step detection proved reliable in structured laboratory settings across most sensor locations and clinical cohorts, whereas unsupervised free-living monitoring produced a substantial degradation for most algorithms. Over all conditions, the three evaluated time–frequency methods obtained the best average ranks for detection accuracy, step-duration error and cadence error.</jats:p>

results.title: Disease-modifying interventions in psychiatry
results.summary: <jats:p>Disease-modifying interventions do not just treat the symptoms of the disease but target the underlying disease process and natural course. The construct of disease-modifying treatments has transformed the care of disorders, like rheumatoid arthritis and multiple sclerosis, by shifting the focus to preventing end-organ damage rather than offering symptomatic treatment. As mental illness may have a chronic and progressive course, there is a need to consider whether any of our interventions may be disease-modifying. We, therefore, conducted a search using databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE and PsycINFO, to identify peer-reviewed papers and grey literature related to the research question: ‘Which psychiatric treatments are disease-modifying?’ Disease-modifying properties were largely operationalised around end-organ changes, including structural brain changes evident on neuroimaging and cognition, and were reported for conventional psychotropics, as well as for novel pharmaceuticals and non-pharmacological interventions. Lithium and electroconvulsive therapy showed the greatest evidence as disease-modifying interventions. However, to establish this and identify potential other disease-modifying treatments, there needs to be a shift in the focus of psychiatric clinical trials to include primary outcomes that reflect disease progression and not just acute symptom burden. The potential disease-modifying properties of lithium and electroconvulsive therapy should spur the prioritisation of treatment higher up the algorithm, as well as the commencement of disease-modifying therapy as early as possible in the illness course to prevent adverse outcomes.</jats:p>

results.title: A Central-Vein-Sign-Aware Deep-Learning Pipeline for Lesion Detection and Automated CVS Assessment on Brain SWIp: An Exploratory End-to-End Feasibility Study
results.summary: <jats:p>The central vein sign (CVS) is a supportive imaging biomarker for multiple sclerosis (MS), but its manual assessment on susceptibility-weighted imaging with phase enhancement (SWIp) is time-consuming and reader-dependent. Existing automated methods rely on multi-contrast volumetric data and prerequisite lesion masks. We study a deliberately different formulation: a structured end-to-end pipeline operating on a single axial SWIp sequence with sparse slice-wise annotations and no prerequisite volumetric mask, combining anatomical tiling, tiled lesion detection, cross-slice reconstruction of lesion identity, and two complementary branches that independently assess the same lesion crops—direct CVS classification (Pathway A) and vein-presence gating, vein segmentation, and geometric centrality (Pathway B). A cohort of 64 clinical studies annotated by four readers was merged into a consolidated reference. The main contribution is an explicit decomposition of where such a pipeline fails. On an eight-study evaluation, the pipeline recovered 78 of 111 reference lesions (70.3%); lesion-level F1 was 0.667 for Pathway A and 0.706 for Pathway B, rising to 0.785 and 0.818 when restricted to detected lesions, and a paired test found no significant difference between the pathways (p=1.00). Detection is therefore the binding constraint, and a threshold sweep shows the associated overcounting of CVS-positive lesions is not separable from it by detector confidence alone. All operating thresholds were selected on these same eight studies, which were acquired on a single scanner, so the figures are single-centre development-set estimates rather than measures of clinical performance and are likely optimistic. Larger-cohort, acquisition-diverse independent evaluation is required before clinical use.</jats:p>

results.title: Blood Cell Imaging Analysis for Multiple Sclerosis Classification Using Leave-One-Subject-Out Study with Deep Neural Networks
results.summary: <jats:p>Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic neurological disease whose diagnosis typically relies on resource-intensive and partly invasive procedures such as MRI and spinal fluid analysis. This study explores whether deep learning can identify distinguishing patterns in RBC images associated with MS, aiming to determine whether blood-cell imaging may provide information relevant to understanding the disease. The initial dataset comprised 121 images from 13 independent subjects. To expand the dataset to 1944 images, image augmentation techniques were applied to the training data to increase image variability. Due to the small dataset, training was carried out using a Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) strategy to assess model performance on unseen subjects. Four deep learning architectures, VGG16, DenseNet201, MobileNetV2, and the Swin Transformer, were evaluated using subject-level Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV). The Swin Transformer achieved the highest mean accuracy (73.53%), followed by the fully fine-tuned VGG16 (71.02%). Explainable AI techniques (Grad-CAM and SWTformer-v1) applied to the given dataset showed that VGG16 focused on broader structural patterns in cell groupings, while SWTformer-v1 attended to more localized regions. These findings suggest that deep-learning models can identify distinguishing image patterns that contribute to classifying RBC images from MS and healthy controls. The XAI analyses further provide insight into the image regions the models use, although their biological relevance requires validation in larger cohorts.</jats:p>
